<div class="clt-lesson batch-lesson" data-lesson="anova"><h2 id="learning-goals">What are we trying to understand?</h2><p><strong>How large are differences between groups relative to the variation within groups?</strong></p><p>A researcher compares attention scores across three independent study-strategy groups. Each group has eight illustrative scores. Move the group centers apart or increase individual variability while keeping the other feature fixed.</p><div class="clt-overview"><strong>Learning goals</strong><ol><li>Distinguish between-group and within-group variation.</li><li>Explain the F statistic as a ratio of mean squares.</li><li>Interpret the omnibus p-value and effect size without claiming which groups differ.</li><li>Identify the assumptions and need for follow-up comparisons.</li></ol></div><h2 id="explore">Make a prediction and explore</h2><section class="clt-simulator"><p>Predict what happens to F when the groups move apart without changing their within-group spread.</p><div class="controls"><div><label for="gap">Distance of outer group means from 50: <output id="gap-v">4</output></label><input id="gap" type="range" min="0" max="12" step="1" value="4"></div><div><label for="spread">Within-group spread multiplier: <output id="spread-v">1</output></label><input id="spread" type="range" min="0.5" max="3" step="0.5" value="1"></div></div><div class="metrics"><div class="metric"><span>F statistic</span><strong id="f">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Omnibus p-value</span><strong id="p">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Eta squared (η²)</span><strong id="eta">—</strong></div></div><div id="chart" class="plot"></div><p class="note">Dots are individual scores; orange marks label group means. Score scale is fixed.</p><table class="data-table"><caption>ANOVA decomposition</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Source</th><th scope="col">SS</th><th scope="col">df</th><th scope="col">MS</th></tr></thead><tbody id="anova-table"></tbody></table><p id="decision" role="status"></p><details><summary>View all scores</summary><p id="data"></p></details></section><h2 id="interpret">Interpret what you find</h2><ol><li>Set gap to 0 and change spread. Explain why F remains zero.</li><li>Set gap to 4 and compare spread 0.5 and 3. Which design provides clearer evidence of mean differences?</li><li>Hold spread fixed and increase gap. Record F and eta squared.</li><li>Explain why a significant omnibus result does not tell us which pair differs.</li></ol><h2 id="explanation">What is the method telling us?</h2><p>One-way ANOVA evaluates H₀: all population means are equal. Between-group sum of squares weights squared differences of group means from the grand mean. Within-group sum of squares measures squared deviations around each group mean.</p><div class="formula">F = MS between / MS within<br>MS = SS / degrees of freedom<br>η² = SS between / SS total</div><p>A large F is evidence against H₀ under the model. The F distribution is right-skewed and the p-value is its upper tail. Classical ANOVA assumes independent observations, approximately normal within-group errors and equal population variances. The examples use equal group sizes and equal spreads; they illustrate the calculation rather than providing random experimental evidence. If the omnibus test is significant, use planned contrasts or appropriately adjusted follow-up comparisons to identify differences.</p><h2 id="knowledge-check">Check your understanding</h2><p>Choose an answer, then check your reasoning.
